research_question: When does spherical-cap pruning reduce query latency against the same rowwise float64 scoring kernel while preserving bitwise scores and ordered IDs?
hypothesis: Tight separated clusters permit substantial pruning; isotropic high-dimensional vectors and small databases can be slower due to loose caps and dispatch overhead.
measurement: Each mode gets the same single-query API, k, float64 vectors, thread count, and queries. Randomize mode and query order per repetition. Timer includes input validation, normalization, bounds, vector scoring, top-k, and result allocation, excludes data generation/build/load. Build, load, serialization and first call recorded separately. Report median and IQR over all query samples and per-repeat medians; no tail-latency claim. All valid samples retained. Existing seven cases retain their original positions/seeds; the 500-row scale is appended. Cross-size cases use different seeds and are workload coverage, not a controlled scaling law. Old/current timings must not be pooled.
not_claimed: speedup over BLAS with the corrected rowwise kernel
historical timing valid for changed source
bitwise equality across NumPy versions or hardware
revision_reason: Candidate scoring changed from shape-dependent BLAS matvec to a shared nonoptimized einsum kernel after a legal-input near-tie counterexample. This is a new measurement, not validation of historical 10.20x BLAS-relative speedup.
scoring_kernel: numpy.einsum("ij,j->i", vectors, query, optimize=False); same kernel for scan/blocked/pruned; no claim against an optimized BLAS scan
